summary: Specifies the Diameter base protocol, a framework for authentication, authorization, and accounting for uses such as network access and IP mobility, in both local and roaming situations. It defines the message format, transport, error handling, and security. It is a proposed standard and was replaced by RFC 6733.

plainLanguage.summary: When you connect, someone must check who you are, what you may do, and keep a tally. Diameter is the language servers use for that. This memo is its main rulebook.

questions: what is an avp in diameter
subtitle: The base AAA protocol that lets network access devices ask servers who a user is, what they may do, and what they used.

tldr.problem: RADIUS-era AAA protocols lacked defined failover, reliable transport, mandatory transmission security, explicit agents, server-initiated messages and capability negotiation, which strained larger and roaming networks.
tldr.mechanism: Diameter is a peer-to-peer protocol over TCP or SCTP on port 3868. Peers exchange capabilities, then send requests and answers made of typed AVPs, routed by realm through relay, proxy, redirect and translation agents, with IPsec or TLS on every connection.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3588 supplies the base protocol and accounting that every Diameter application builds on. It has been obsoleted by RFC 6733 and was updated by RFC 5719, RFC 5729 and RFC 6408.

today: RFC 3588 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 6733, which is now the Diameter base protocol specification. It was also updated by RFC 5719, RFC 5729 and RFC 6408.

sections.title: Why Diameter Replaced RADIUS-Style AAA
sections.content:
Authentication, Authorization and Accounting (AAA) protocols such as TACACS and RADIUS were first deployed for dial-up PPP and terminal server access. As wireless, DSL, Mobile IP and Ethernet arrived, access servers grew more complex and put new demands on AAA.

The RFC lists what RADIUS left open and how Diameter answers it:

  • Failover: Diameter adds application-layer acknowledgements and defined failover algorithms.
  • Transport: it runs over reliable TCP or SCTP rather than UDP with undefined retransmission.
  • Security: IPsec support is mandatory and TLS is optional, applied to every connection.
  • Agents: proxies, redirects and relays have explicit, defined behavior.
  • Server-initiated messages: support is mandatory, so a server can ask for re-authorization or abort a session.
  • Capabilities and errors: peers negotiate capabilities, report errors, and mark attributes as mandatory or not.
  • Peer discovery and roaming: peers can be found through DNS, and inter-domain routing is built in.

Diameter does not share a PDU with RADIUS, but the RFC says considerable effort went into allowing both to be deployed in the same network, for example through gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: An older system for checking who may use the network had gaps, like no plan if a helper computer broke. Diameter fills those gaps with clear rules.

sections.title: Peers, Applications and Agents
sections.content:
Any Diameter node can start a request, so the protocol is peer to peer. A client is an edge device that enforces access control, such as a Network Access Server (NAS). A server authenticates and authorizes for a realm. An agent forwards or answers without deciding locally, and comes in four kinds:

  • Relay: routes by realm, changes only routing information, and must advertise the Relay application so it can carry any application.
  • Proxy: also routes, but applies policy and can modify messages, so it must understand the applications it advertises. Because it modifies messages, it prevents end-to-end security.
  • Redirect: does not forward at all; it answers with the address of the server to contact directly.
  • Translation: converts between Diameter and another AAA protocol such as RADIUS, and must keep session state.

The base protocol covers capabilities negotiation, message delivery and accounting. For authentication and authorization it is always extended by an application. Two are named in this RFC and specified elsewhere: NASREQ (identifier 1) and Mobile IPv4 (identifier 2). Every message carries an Application Identifier, and each application needs an IANA-assigned one.

The RFC separates a connection (a transport link between two peers) from a session (an application-layer user session identified by a Session-Id, which can span several connections). Messages for many sessions are multiplexed over one connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers ask the questions, some give the answers, and some just pass notes along or point to the right desk. They all follow the same school rules.

sections.title: The Diameter Header and AVPs
sections.content:
Each message is a header followed by AVPs (attribute-value pairs). The header holds a Version (which MUST be 1), a three-octet Message Length, eight command flags, a three-octet Command-Code, a four-octet Application-ID, and two 32-bit identifiers. The flags are R (request), P (proxiable), E (error) and T (potentially re-transmitted).

The Hop-by-Hop Identifier matches answers to requests on one connection, and agents replace it with a local value and restore it on the answer. The End-to-End Identifier detects duplicates, must stay unique for at least 4 minutes even across reboots, and MUST NOT be modified by agents.

All data travels in AVPs. Each AVP header has an AVP Code, flags V, M and P, a three-octet length and an optional Vendor-ID. Codes 1 to 255 are kept for RADIUS compatibility. The M bit means support is mandatory: a client, server, proxy or translation agent MUST reject a message holding an unrecognized AVP with M set, while relays and redirect agents MUST NOT. The P bit asks for encryption for end-to-end security, and V says a vendor ID is present. Data types include OctetString, Integer32, Integer64, Unsigned32, Unsigned64, Float32, Float64 and Grouped, which holds other AVPs. Values are padded to 32-bit boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message has a label on top saying what it is and where it is going, and then a list of small labelled facts, like a form with boxes.

sections.title: Transport, Discovery and Capabilities Exchange
sections.content:
Diameter runs on port 3868 over TCP and SCTP. Clients MUST support one of them and agents and servers MUST support both; when connecting, SCTP SHOULD be tried first. If no connection exists, an attempt SHOULD be made periodically, and the Tc timer recommends 30 seconds.

Peers can be found by static configuration (which every node MUST support), by SLPv2, or by DNS using NAPTR and SRV records. A discovered peer must also be checked as authorized for its role, since an authenticated certificate alone does not prove that.

When a connection comes up, the peers MUST exchange Capabilities-Exchange-Request and Capabilities-Exchange-Answer messages (CER and CEA, command code 257). These carry the sender's identity, IP addresses and supported applications and security. With no common application, the answer carries DIAMETER_NO_COMMON_APPLICATION, and with no common security, DIAMETER_NO_COMMON_SECURITY. CER and CEA are never proxied or relayed.

The peer state machine MUST be followed by every implementation, with stable states Closed, I-Open and R-Open. If both sides connect at once, an election keeps one connection by comparing Origin-Host values. Device-Watchdog-Request and Answer (code 280) detect transport failures, and Disconnect-Peer-Request and Answer (code 282) end a connection politely. On failure, pending requests go to an alternate agent with the T flag set, and receivers use the End-to-End Identifier with Origin-Host to spot duplicates.
sections.plainLanguage: When two computers first connect, they say hello and swap lists of what they can do. They also check on each other now and then, and if one goes quiet the work moves to a backup.

sections.title: Routing, Sessions, Accounting and Errors
sections.content:
Routing. Requests that agents may forward carry a Destination-Realm AVP and an application identifier AVP. Each node first checks if the request is for itself, then if the Destination-Host is a direct peer, then routes by realm using its Realm Routing Table, whose local actions are LOCAL, RELAY, PROXY and REDIRECT. Failing all that, it answers with DIAMETER_UNABLE_TO_DELIVER. Relays and proxies add a Route-Record AVP and MUST answer DIAMETER_LOOP_DETECTED if they find their own identity in one.

Errors. Result-Code values fall in classes: 1xxx informational, 2xxx success (DIAMETER_SUCCESS is 2001), 3xxx protocol errors, 4xxx transient failures and 5xxx permanent failures. Protocol errors are carried in answers with the E bit set.

Sessions. The base protocol defines no authorization request, since that is application-specific, but it does define session control. A server can send Re-Auth-Request (258) to demand re-authentication, and Abort-Session-Request (274) to stop a session. The access device sends Session-Termination-Request (275) when a stateful session ends. The Session-Id MUST be globally and eternally unique and begins with the sender's identity. Authorization-Lifetime and Auth-Grace-Period bound how long service may continue.

Accounting. The model is server directed, with real-time delivery; batch accounting is not supported. The client sends Accounting-Request and receives Accounting-Answer (271). The server steers behavior with Acct-Interim-Interval and Accounting-Realtime-Required. Clients should keep records in non-volatile memory until acknowledged, and duplicates are detected using the Session-Id and Accounting-Record-Number pair.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages are passed along using the address of the target office. If something goes wrong, the answer comes with a number that says what kind of problem it was. The system also keeps a tally of how much you used.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Diameter MUST NOT be used without a security mechanism, and every connection MUST use IPsec or TLS. Clients MUST support IPsec and MAY support TLS, and servers MUST support both. If a connection is not protected by IPsec, the CER/CEA exchange MUST include an Inband-Security-ID AVP with the value TLS, and the handshake begins after that exchange. Failure of the handshake closes both ends.

The RFC suggests IPsec mainly at the edges and inside a domain, possibly with pre-shared keys, and TLS between domains. IPsec cannot set trusted root CAs per application, whereas TLS can, so TLS SHOULD protect connections between administrative domains. TLS peers MUST mutually authenticate, and nodes MUST be able to negotiate TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_MD5, TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_SHA and TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA.

Hop-by-hop security does not protect a session across relays or proxies, so an end-to-end security extension is described outside this RFC and is strongly RECOMMENDED. Path authorization matters too: a home server must check the Route-Record AVPs before authorizing, and may refuse requests routed through an untrusted realm with DIAMETER_AUTHORIZATION_REJECTED.
sections.plainLanguage: All the talking must happen in a locked tunnel. Computers also have to check that whoever is on the other end is really allowed to do that job.

fields.desc: R, P, E, T and four reserved bits.
